nodes.text: Resistivity depends on temperature — usually in metals

(Superconductors — materials with zero resistance — are generally extremely low temperature. “High temperature” superconductors are those which exhibit R = 0 above 77 K, the boiling point of nitrogen.)

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: I equals V divided by R

nodes.detailed_figure_description: An I-versus-V coordinate graph has current I on the vertical axis and voltage V on the horizontal axis. Two blue straight lines pass through the origin with different positive slopes. Above the graph is the relation I = (1/R)V. A blue note to the right says that as R increases, delta I over delta V decreases.
nodes.figure_alternative: I-versus-V graph for ohmic materials, showing straight lines through the origin and a smaller slope for greater resistance.

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: I equals one over R times V
As R increases, delta I over delta V decreases

nodes.text: Example In the circuit below, is V higher at point A or B? What about I?

nodes.detailed_figure_description: A single-loop circuit contains a resistor in the top wire between labeled points A on the left and B on the right. An orange arrow above the resistor points from A toward B and is labeled I. A battery is in the bottom wire, with its positive terminal on the left and negative terminal on the right.
nodes.figure_alternative: Series circuit with current flowing from A through a resistor to B; the battery is positive on the left and negative on the right.

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: V equals I R, so V sub A is greater than V sub B
